A generic `ForkSessionRequest` derives the source session's active labels before creating the child, unions them with any explicitly supplied child labels, and persists the effective set in child metadata. The `session.forked` event reports only the source-derived set as `inherited_taint_labels`; a fork cannot clear source taint merely by omitting request metadata or changing agents. Resume and tool execution seed policy state from that durable session metadata, so the boundary remains enforced after restart. Custom policies implement `authorize(ToolPolicyRequest) -> ToolPolicyResult`.

Denied tool calls are recoverable by default. The runtime emits one terminal `tool.call.blocked`, does not run the protected operation, appends an error `tool_result` to the provider-neutral transcript, and lets the model continue. A direct `ToolPolicy` refusal discovered while planning a paused multi-call round has no `tool.call.started`; direct refusals checked at the per-call execution boundary and the nested `CommandPolicy` used by `ExecCommandTool` occur after `tool.call.started`. The terminal event is canonical for both refusal paths: its payload carries `denied_by` (`tool_policy` or `command_policy`), `decision`, a safe `reason`, `metadata`, `tool_name`, `tool_call_id`, the complete `model_step_id` / `model_attempt_id` / `tool_round_id` execution identity, `idempotency_key`, and the redacted model-facing `result`. `metadata` contains the `ToolPolicyResult` metadata for a tool-policy refusal and is an empty object for a command-policy refusal, whose result type has no metadata surface. Policy-denial reasons and model-facing refusal text are bounded to 4 KiB of UTF-8; longer values end with `[policy denial reason truncated]` without splitting a Unicode scalar. A command refusal never also emits `tool.call.failed`, so event queries, SSE replay, logging, tracing, and recovery count one terminal outcome. The denial payload does not copy command arguments, environment values, stdin, credentials, or hook-modified effective arguments; policy authors must likewise keep reasons and `ToolPolicy.metadata` free of secrets. Configured secret redaction still applies, but bounding is not semantic sanitization. Tools whose registered contract disables argument publication apply a stronger rule: policy reasons and metadata plus before/after-hook outputs, diagnostics, and actions are replaced with fixed operational classifications because an extension can derive them from withheld input even when no configured secret matches it. A before-tool hook block still uses `tool.call.blocked` with `blocked_by=before_tool_call_hook`, but it is not a policy refusal and therefore has no `denied_by`. If a before-tool hook modifies arguments and policy reauthorization refuses them, the event remains a policy denial with `denied_by=tool_policy` and also carries `blocked_by=tool_policy_reauthorization` to identify the second gate. Tool policy implementation errors are not policy refusals and retain their existing failure behavior. Existing stored events and checkpoints are not rewritten.

Policies may also return `ToolPolicyDecision.REQUIRE_APPROVAL`. This is a durable interrupt, not an in-memory UI callback. The runtime authorizes the model's whole tool-call round before execution and durably replaces the unplanned round with its policy-evaluated call records. Each call records explicit policy evidence: `authoritative` for a durable policy decision, `unregistered` when no registered tool existed at planning time, and `ambiguous` when recovery cannot prove the result of an interrupted evaluation. If any authoritative call requires approval, the same checkpoint transaction retains that planned `pending_tool_round` and adds its matching `pending_tool_approval`; there is no state in which the policy-required round has been removed but its approval has not been published. The runtime then emits `session.checkpointed`, emits `tool.call.approval_requested`, marks the session `interrupted`, and emits `session.interrupted` with `interruption_type="tool_approval_required"`. No tool implementation in that round runs before approval. If a process stops before policy publication, recovery does not replay `authorize()`: stateful or time-sensitive policy evaluation is not guaranteed to reproduce the lost result. Instead, every registered call without a complete recognized durable decision is recorded as non-authoritative `ambiguous`, and the claimed recovery atomically publishes a manual gate before it may close the round. Approving that gate acknowledges recovery but records each ambiguous call as `tool.call.blocked`; it never emits `tool.call.approved` or `tool.call.started` and never dispatches the tool. A call recorded as `unregistered` also remains non-executable if a later deployment registers that name. Recovery validates transcript integrity and routes structured-output rounds before publishing the gate, so malformed or runtime-owned rounds cannot expose an executable approval surface. The same rule applies to unversioned legacy rounds, while recognized legacy decisions remain authoritative: recovery cannot downgrade a lost or recorded `DENY`, a policy exception, or missing evidence into executable approval. A versioned round marked `planned` is rejected if its evidence and decision conflict; the marker or absence of a decision is never authorization.

Callers resolve pending approvals with `CayuApp.resolve_tool_approval(ToolApprovalRequest(...))`. Both resolution request types require `approval_id`, `tool_round_id`, and the effective `tool_call_id`. The store verifies those values against the complete paired approval/round snapshot in the same transaction that claims `interrupted → running` and advances the run epoch. The same private coordination state binds a canonical digest of the approval request's decision, reason, metadata, and resolver actor. A stale resolver therefore cannot claim a session that has paused again on another approval merely because its status is again `interrupted`, and a same-decision retry with changed audit or authority data cannot execute under an earlier grant. Approval emits `session.resumed` and emits `tool.call.approved` only for authoritatively approval-gated calls. Public approval events and pending-action projections omit the private pre-execution arguments retained by the paired checkpoint. The request digest is not included in public events: once the private intent matches, grant replay uses the event's exact approval, round, and call identities, while bounded or redacted audit fields never decide replay authority. The runtime then runs only calls with durable executable authority, appends the finalized safe assistant-call message and grouped tool-result message, clears the exact paired approval and round, and continues the model loop. Ambiguous recovery gates are deliberately approval-shaped for operator visibility, but their positive action is labelled as safe continuation in the dashboard and produces blocked results rather than authorization. Denial emits `session.resumed`, does not execute the interrupted round, appends the same safe assistant/result pair for the round, clears the same exact pair, and continues the model loop. Those transcript messages, the exact checkpoint clear, and causal `session.checkpointed` event are committed with an insert-only `approval-close:{approval_id}` runtime-publication receipt. A lost acknowledgement is reconciled from that exact receipt; an identical request returns the durable closure without rebinding an environment or dispatching a tool, while a conflicting approval identity, decision, reason, metadata, or resolver actor fails closed. Limit-triggered closure carries the original requested decision and request digest even though its operational stop decision is `limit_reached`.

When a `ResumeRequest` discovers an interrupted raw round and must first publish a recovered fail-closed approval, its new messages are retained as private deferred interaction input and referenced by the pending round instead of being appended after the unresolved assistant tool call. Resolution first publishes the finalized safe assistant-call message when it was quarantined, followed by exactly one grouped tool-result message, while atomically clearing the exact approval/round pair. Only after that durable close does it idempotently materialize the deferred input and build the next provider request. Ordinary tool-round receipts describe that complete safe transcript closure; if a process stops between close and materialization, receipt replay or incomplete-session recovery finishes the retained tail without losing, reordering, or duplicating it. Approval retry uses stored terminal tool events for the same approval as the execution ledger: completed, failed, blocked, or approval-denied tool results are reused and never re-executed, but the exact request digest must still match before the retry can advance. An ambiguous blocked result also binds the recovery acknowledgement, so a retry cannot reinterpret it as a different decision or substitute different audit data. Durable resolution attempts, grants, denials, or terminal outcomes written before request digests existed are not used to infer request identity from their bounded and redacted event representations; automatic resolution remains interrupted before environment binding or tool execution. A pre-digest resolution intent is likewise loadable for diagnosis but is not upgraded into new authority.

If a tool has `tool.call.started` for that approval without a terminal event, Cayu leaves the session `interrupted` with `manual_recovery_required` instead of re-running a side-effecting tool whose outcome is unknown. The caller can then use `CayuApp.recover_tool_approval(ToolApprovalRecoveryRequest(...))` to mark the externally verified outcome as `completed` or `failed` and provide the exact message the model should see. Recovery performs the same atomic approval and intent claim and persists the caller-supplied message as the terminal tool result. It closes the exact approval pair and continues only when every call in the round now has a terminal outcome and the claimed modern intent supplies the original request digest. Recovery never treats its own reason, metadata, or actor as authority to run a remaining sibling; when any call remains unresolved, the verified result stays durable, the approval remains interrupted, and an exact retry of the original `ToolApprovalRequest` is required before pending work can execute. Cayu does not infer domain facts for recovery. Normal `ResumeRequest` rejects sessions with pending tool approvals because provider histories require the assistant tool-call round to be followed by matching tool results before any later conversation.

Legacy private `tool.call.approval_requested` events may nest the complete
approval under `event.payload["approval"]`. Current durable and public events
retain the typed approval descriptor but set `arguments_state="quarantined"`
and omit executable arguments for the gating call and every sibling. Both
representations repeat `approval_id`,
`tool_call_id`, `model_step_id`, `model_attempt_id`, and `tool_round_id` at the
payload root. Those representations must agree. `PendingToolApproval.from_event`
parses only complete legacy events; it rejects quarantined events rather than
fabricating empty arguments. `PendingToolApprovalEventView.from_event` parses
either representation and exposes `arguments=None` with the explicit
quarantined state when arguments are unavailable. Public application streams expose field-scoped aliases
for the actionable `approval_id`, `tool_round_id`, and `tool_call_id`. Pass
those aliases directly to the resolution or recovery request: the public
`CayuApp` method resolves each one against the exact durable event and session
before any coordination decision. Non-actionable execution identities remain
private markers.

The two approval-event view models detach their JSON arguments and metadata at
construction. A `PendingToolApprovalEventView` also detaches each supplied
`PendingToolCallApprovalEventView`, so later mutation of a previously validated
call view cannot rewrite the round-level approval projection. Its mutable
continuation contracts (`structured_output`, `limits`, and `budget_limits`) are
likewise rebuilt as validated owned snapshots. `ThinkingConfig` is revalidated
into the exact frozen base contract, while `RetryPolicy` uses its canonical
exact-type immutable boundary; mutable subclasses of either are rejected.

`ToolApprovalRequest.decision` uses `ToolApprovalDecision`; manual recovery uses
`ToolApprovalRecoveryOutcome`. These enums are the public typed values for the
binary approval and externally verified recovery outcomes described above.

Every resolution and recovery request (approval and user-input alike) accepts an optional typed `resolved_by: ResolutionActor` (`subject`, optional `tenant`, `source`, JSON-safe `claims`) — the audit provenance field, distinct from the caller-claimed free-form `reason`/`metadata`. The actor's `subject`/`tenant`/`source` are stamped inside the resolution event payloads at emission (never derived from app-side state): `session.resumed` for all four resolution/recovery paths, `tool.call.approved`, `tool.call.approval_denied`, both manual-recovery terminal events, and the injected `ask_user` `tool.call.completed`. `claims` stay on the request for in-process use and are never persisted into event payloads — they carry deployment authorization state, and event payloads are not redacted. Policy-attributed `tool.call.blocked` events deliberately carry the policy's attribution, not the resolver's — join via `approval_id`. `source` records how the identity claim was established, and only certain layers may produce each value: `http_auth` is minted exclusively by the server from a verified `AuthContext` (on an auth-configured server, a request body carrying `resolved_by` is rejected with 400); `request` marks caller-asserted identity (direct SDK calls, or open-access HTTP bodies, whose `source` the server always re-stamps to `request`); `system` marks runtime-generated actors, and subjects prefixed `cayu:` are reserved for them (mirroring the reserved label namespace). Direct SDK callers are a trusted boundary and may construct system actors; HTTP bodies cannot.

A policy demanding approval can also bound how long that demand stays valid: `ToolPolicyResult.approval_expires_in_seconds` (or `AlwaysRequireApprovalToolPolicy(expires_in_seconds=...)`) is converted to an absolute timezone-aware `expires_at` on the `pending_tool_approval` checkpoint (visible in the `tool.call.approval_requested` and `session.interrupted` payloads via the approval dump). A session carrying that pending approval cannot be forked; resolve the approval before branching rather than using a fork to extend or duplicate its lifetime. Expiry is evaluated at access time by the resolution winner after the atomic `interrupted → running` claim — there is no background sweeper, and the pure `pending_approval_expired` helper centralizes the lifecycle decision; the clock basis is wall-clock UTC across workers. An expired resolution is deterministic regardless of the requested decision: the runtime emits `tool.call.approval_expired` once (payload carries `expires_at`, the caller's `requested_decision`, the system actor as `resolved_by`, and the caller's actor as `triggered_by`), then runs the ordinary denial path with `expired: true` on each `tool.call.approval_denied` event and on `session.resumed`. Expiry gates the first grant only: an exact retry backed by a modern request digest honors the in-window grant instead of coercing it to denial. A pre-digest grant still fails closed because its original request identity cannot be proved. Manual recovery is not blocked by expiry because it reconciles a side effect that only starts after a grant; out-of-window retries and recoveries are stamped `expired: true` for the audit trail. Pending user input does not expire.

The approval primitive stays binary and single-party on purpose. Multi-tier business approvals — a product-computed routing tier deciding who may resolve, and approve/condition/decline outcomes mapped onto the binary decision with an audit projection of the business outcome next to the runtime decision — are an additive adapter over this surface: `TieredApprovalPolicy`, `resolve_business_approval`, and `business_approval_audit` in `cayu.runtime.business_approvals`. The audit projection treats equivalent enum-valued and plain-string known event types identically while preserving its fail-closed handling of malformed, contradictory, or identity-mismatched evidence. The adapter's tier gate is an application affordance enforced in the calling process, not a runtime security boundary (pass `resolved_by` for authenticated provenance); semantics live in the [business approvals recipe](recipes/business-approvals.md).

The built-in `ask_user` tool (`UserInputTool`, opt-in — register it only on agents that should be able to ask) lets a model pause mid-run for user input, reusing the same durable pause/resume machinery as approvals. It is recognized before execution: if a round contains an `ask_user` call with a usable question, Cayu atomically replaces the pending round with a `pending_user_input` checkpoint, including any private quarantined assistant turn, and inserts the exact `user-input-open:{input_id}` receipt with the `session.checkpointed` and `session.awaiting_user_input` events. The pause identity binds the session incarnation, source interaction and run epoch, input/tool/round/model identities, execution-profile fingerprint, and content digest. Cayu then marks the session `interrupted` and emits `session.interrupted` with `interruption_type="user_input_required"` (whose private payload carries the full `user_input`; public event and pending-action projections omit pre-execution arguments). As with approval, no tool in that round runs before the pause. A stored-event consumer detects an input pause from that `session.interrupted` event, not from `session.awaiting_user_input` — both are emitted on the pause, and `interrupted` is the durable terminal one. The caller answers with `CayuApp.resolve_user_input(UserInputResponse(session_id=…, input_id=…, answer=…))`: Cayu atomically claims the exact pause and answer digest while moving the session to a new run epoch, emits `session.resumed`, injects the answer as the `ask_user` tool result (`ask_user.run` never executes — the runtime owns the result), and runs any other tool calls in the same round (none ran before the pause). Closure atomically appends the finalized safe assistant call message and grouped tool-result message in model order, clears both the pause and answer claim, binds the exact lifecycle events, and inserts `user-input-close:{input_id}`. The `ask_user` tool is `parallel_safe=False`, so it never runs inside a concurrent batch. Like a pending approval, the original run's config (`max_steps`, `limits`, `budget_limits`, `retry_policy`) is persisted on the `pending_user_input` checkpoint and restored on resume. Resolution fields may restate that configuration, but a changed provider, budget, structured-output, thinking, or finalization value is execution-profile drift and is rejected before status transition, tool execution, or provider dispatch. `resolve_user_input` is a dedicated single-purpose API (no approve/deny); a session awaiting user input is preserved across worker-startup recovery (a crash mid-pause is finalized with `interruption_type="user_input_required"` and reported as a `pending_user_input` recovery action, so the question stays discoverable), rejected by normal `resume(...)` (answer it first), and rejected by `fork` (answer it first). The optional server exposes `POST /api/user-input/resolve` and `POST /api/user-input/recover`. Resume applies the same guards as approval resolution: a denied co-round tool is blocked (not executed), the run's `structured_output` contract cannot be swapped by the resolver, and a retry after a mid-resume failure reuses already-recorded terminal outcomes (a tool that already ran is not re-executed). `resolve_user_input` is content-bound and idempotent per `input_id`: a lost acknowledgement or identical retry replays the exact closure receipt, while any changed answer or other decision-bearing field conflicts without mutation. Before reconnecting an environment, publishing recovery evidence, running hooks, or dispatching sibling tools, an answer or manual-recovery claim atomically advances from `claimed` to `executing`. An external operator interruption can atomically supersede either the active pause or a pre-execution claim, clear both checkpoint roots, and carry an exact typed supersession marker into the interruption evidence; the losing pre-execution resolver cannot dispatch continuation work or clear a later pause. If execution admission commits first, interruption fails closed without publishing supersession, and the exact execution owner remains fenced until it reaches a definite outcome. Recovery classifies a pause only from positive open, answering, close, or supersession evidence and fails closed when those representations are missing or conflict. If a co-round tool started on a prior resume but has no terminal event (a crash mid-tool), the retry does not silently re-run it — it stops with `session.interrupted` carrying `manual_recovery_required` and the stuck `tool_call_id`. The caller then supplies the externally verified outcome with `CayuApp.recover_user_input(UserInputRecoveryRequest(session_id=…, input_id=…, answer=…, tool_call_id=…, outcome=…, message=…))` (mirroring `recover_tool_approval`): Cayu persists the caller-supplied message as that tool's terminal result, re-supplies the `answer` in case the `ask_user` result was not recorded before the crash, and continues the round. Cayu does not infer the outcome itself. Two v1 limitations: a round that mixes `ask_user` with a tool that requires approval pauses for approval first (the `ask_user` question is not asked that round), and only the first `ask_user` in a round pauses; and the paused round's remaining tools run on resume without a fresh budget projection (the round was projected against limits when it paused).

Ordinary tool rounds are also crash-recoverable. When a model step produces normal executable tool calls, Cayu atomically stores the assistant tool-call message as private quarantined checkpoint state and creates `pending_tool_round` before executing tools; it does not append that raw assistant message to the model-visible transcript yet. The same checkpoint initializes a separate safe publication projection: tool arguments are unavailable, ordinary text is redacted, provider-owned opaque protocol state is retained byte-for-byte only while the known secret scope proves that no redaction would change it, and the original environment's dynamic-secret capability is recorded for recovery. A concrete environment is dynamic when it exposes a vault or credential proxy. A factory-backed environment is conservatively dynamic even when its CREATE result exposes neither, because a later RECONNECT may change those capabilities; no immutable factory capability contract exists in v1. A durable `tool.call.started` records the authoritative call identity, idempotency key, effect, and `arguments_state="quarantined"`, but never the model-authored argument object. Each invocation receives the original private arguments and owns a distinct secret tracker. A successful vault or credential-proxy resolution atomically applies its updated redactor to the durable projection before the resolved value is returned to tool code; if that checkpoint write fails or caller cancellation arrives during it, the tool never receives the value. A dispatched resolver that cannot be proven stopped permanently marks that invocation scope incomplete even when late completion is fenced from mutating publication state. Before publishing that call's terminal event, Cayu seals the tracker and atomically marks that call's projection evidence complete. A projection becomes ready only after every call identity in the round has contributed complete evidence. A secret collision inside opaque provider state blocks the projection instead of partially rewriting a provider signature, encrypted reasoning item, thought signature, or unknown extension; a blocked or incomplete projection cannot be appended to the transcript or sent in another provider request. Once a tracker is sealed, its terminal `tool.call.completed`, `tool.call.failed`, or `tool.call.blocked` event carries either a key-and-value-redacted `arguments` object with `arguments_state="finalized"`, or `arguments_state="unavailable"` when no complete invocation scope exists (including non-executing and abnormal recovery paths).

A dynamic or legacy/unknown multi-call round privately stages each terminal result inside its owning pending-round, pending-approval, or pending-user-input checkpoint instead of publishing it immediately. Every real vault or credential-proxy resolution extends the round's cumulative redactor and atomically reprojects all staged terminals before the resolved value is returned to tool code. Once every call has sealed its invocation scope, Cayu publishes the staged terminal events in model order, runs terminal hooks against the finalized round-wide projection, and closes the transcript using those exact events. Hook completion and the hook-finalized result are checkpointed before terminal append, so acknowledgement loss or restart does not repeat completed hook work. If restart erased a dynamic round's in-process secret registry before a pending hook ran, recovery does not run that hook with incomplete redaction evidence; it publishes a fixed unavailable result instead. A partially staged approval or user-input continuation likewise closes its remaining siblings as not executed rather than re-executing them. This closes the ordering gap where a later sibling identifies a value as secret only after an earlier call finishes, without guessing secrets from model-authored arguments or discarding unrelated output. If recovery cannot prove complete durable scope coverage, staged output fails closed to a fixed unavailable result before any public event, hook, sink, transcript, export, or later provider request sees it.

Before-tool hooks still receive private invocation arguments, but a dynamic or legacy/unknown scope cannot safely publish argument-derived hook output before secret resolution is complete. Cayu therefore exposes fixed failure telemetry for such hooks and rejects their Cayu-owned publication actions (`emit_custom_event`, session dispatch/fork, and task creation) before the tool runs. This restriction applies to single-call and multi-call rounds; direct side effects performed by custom hook code remain the hook author's responsibility. For observational effectful terminals, the artifact/redaction projection is checkpointed while hook work remains pending, then the hook-completed state is recorded separately. Recovery therefore compares durable public evidence with the exact projected stage rather than the earlier private result.

When every terminal outcome and every publication snapshot are ready, Cayu overlays the finalized tool-call arguments onto the durable safe projection and atomically appends that assistant message followed by the grouped tool-result message, clears `pending_tool_round`, binds the exact lifecycle events, and inserts the immutable round receipt. Recovery uses that durable projection; it never attempts to reconstruct opaque provider state from bounded events or from a newly created redactor after process restart. If an interrupted round's opaque provider state cannot be replayed safely, recovery removes it from resumable work while retaining the complete round under `abandoned_unreplayable_tool_round`. A later distinct abandoned round moves the previous current round into ordered `prior_tool_rounds` history and becomes current; retrying archival of the same round is idempotent. Recovery therefore preserves every such round instead of overwriting evidence or crashing because one older abandoned round already exists. Legacy rounds whose assistant message was already published remain readable and recoverable. Tool events for that round include a `tool_round_id`; terminal events with the matching `tool_round_id` and `tool_call_id` are the execution ledger. The runtime also assigns each tool execution a stable `idempotency_key`, exposed on `ToolContext.idempotency_key`, `ToolContext.metadata["idempotency_key"]`, `tool.call.started`, and terminal tool events. Tools that call external APIs can pass that key to downstream idempotent endpoints so crash/retry boundaries do not duplicate side effects. `ToolSpec.effect` classifies replay behavior: `none` creates no externally meaningful durable mutation, `idempotent` may mutate durable state but a stable downstream identity or contract collapses replay, and `external` has a non-idempotent or outcome-ambiguous durable mutation, so generic retry must not assume replay is safe. The value is execution metadata, not authorization; policy still decides whether a call may run. For registered tools, it is visible on `ToolPolicyRequest.tool_effect`, `tool.call.started.payload["effect"]`, and `ToolContext.metadata["tool_effect"]`. Approval opening and closure use the same receipt substrate with `approval-open:{approval_id}` and `approval-close:{approval_id}` identities; a pending approval retains the private quarantined assistant turn and its safe publication projection in the pending-round checkpoint, then publishes the safe assistant/result pair on closure. User-input opening and closure use the equivalent `user-input-open:{input_id}` and `user-input-close:{input_id}` receipt identities; the pending pause and answer claim remain private checkpoint authority until exact closure or explicit supersession. If the process dies before an ordinary round closes, the next run or resume repairs the transcript before adding new messages or building provider context: recorded terminal outcomes are converted into matching safe assistant-call and `tool_result` parts; tool calls with no recorded start event become explicit not-executed error results; tool calls that started but have no usable, unambiguous terminal outcome become explicit unknown-outcome error results. Cayu never re-executes an ordinary tool call during crash recovery. Instead of accepting a synthesized unknown outcome, an operator can reconcile a started-but-unresolved call manually before resuming: `CayuApp.recover_tool_round(ToolRoundRecoveryRequest(session_id=…, round_id=…, tool_call_id=…, outcome=…, message=…))` (HTTP: `POST /api/tool-rounds/recover`) persists the externally verified COMPLETED/FAILED outcome as that call's terminal result and continues the session from it. One call per invocation: while other started-but-unresolved calls remain, the session returns to INTERRUPTED with `manual_recovery_required` naming the next call, and each recovery's persisted result is reused through the round's event ledger. Recovery targets must have durable evidence that execution started but no usable, unambiguous terminal outcome; malformed or contradictory terminal evidence therefore requires manual reconciliation too. Never-started calls keep their deterministic not-executed results, and the tool is never re-executed.

Tools that can mutate the active workspace declare `ToolSpec(workspace_mutation=True, parallel_safe=False)`. Cayu opens an observation window immediately before invocation and closes it after success, failure, timeout, cancellation, or supervisory exit. `parallel_safe=False` serializes the tool inside its own tool round; it is not evidence that another session, process, user, or background service cannot write the workspace. Invocation workspace mutations are owned from dispatch through proven settlement, so cancellation or abandonment of an await does not let thread-, SDK-, or adapter-backed work outlive the closing observation. Workspace methods and runner commands dispatched through the invocation context share that owner: detached calls delay the after observation until they settle, runner cleanup reported as deferred is joined before the after observation, and calls that first start after the window seals are rejected before command execution dispatch. If `SystemExit`, `KeyboardInterrupt`, or `GeneratorExit` leaves the tool while direct workspace work or a runner command is still active, the exact outstanding operation and any subsequent deferred runner cleanup transfer to the environment fence before the signal propagates. Managed-runner deferred settlement delivers a sanitized process-control signal to the active invocation at most once; the unresolved dispatch remains fenced as generic uncertainty for every later waiter. A runner outcome that cannot prove mutation settlement fails the capture with `mutation_settlement_unproven` and terminates the run after preserving the tool's durable terminal outcome; it cannot authorize a receipt or a following tool. That uncertainty is also retained on the process-local registered environment: each concrete factory environment contributes an independent settlement owner, binding finalization cannot synchronize its uncertain workspace, and later factory admission cannot provision or reuse the registration until every outstanding child owner returns exact positive evidence. Static environments retain the equivalent shared-resource fence. The process-local fence proves quiescence only while its owner is alive; the durable lifecycle described below reconstructs evidence status after process loss without treating restart as proof that the old mutation stopped. A supporting `WorkspaceBinding.observe_revision(...)` produces a typed, bounded observation; the compatibility default is explicitly `unsupported`. `DeterministicWorkspaceBinding` supplies a backend-neutral list/read/hash observer, while `GitRepositoryBinding` observes HEAD, branch, the exact index mode and object identity, tracked and untracked worktree state without commits, checkouts, index writes, or other Git mutation. An observation revision is evidence for comparison only: it is not a per-file optimistic concurrency token, a causality claim, or a restorable `WorkspaceSnapshot`.

`workspace.mutation.recorded.attribution` makes that distinction explicit. Its typed confidence is `exclusive_tool`, `concurrent_ambiguity`, or `external_or_unknown`; terminal-only deltas use `unattributed_finalization_change`. Exact tool attribution requires all of: a stable private `Workspace.resource_key`, no overlapping process-observed Cayu mutation window for that resource, and matching `WorkspaceBinding.observe_writer_isolation(...)` evidence with `status="exclusive"`, a non-secret mechanism, and the same lease generation before and after the window. Built-in bindings conservatively return `unknown`, because serial dispatch and process-local locks do not exclude users or sibling processes. Opening a second in-process window marks both receipts ambiguous. The process-local registry also compares the previous completed endpoint with the next window's before observation and records any gap as `pre_window_change` with `external_or_unknown` attribution. It never persists the private resource key.

Direct `ToolContext.workspace` create/replace/delete operations contribute bounded, content-free operation evidence. Cayu reconciles their typed mutation results with independently observed endpoint content identities; a contradiction is retained and prevents exact attribution. Raw paths are replaced with window-scoped SHA-256 identities, result details are content-bound by SHA-256, at most 64 operations participate in reconciliation, and at most 16 appear inline with total/truncation counts. Runner-only mutation remains observable through the revision delta but does not manufacture direct-operation evidence. Attribution, isolation, reconciliation, overlap, gap, and bounded direct-operation projections live in the durable receipt and therefore round-trip unchanged through memory, SQLite, and PostgreSQL stores. Restart does not recreate lost process-local exclusivity; incomplete recovery publishes unknown/ambiguous attribution instead of upgrading it.

`session.forked.workspace_lineage` is separate from transcript and execution-profile lineage. A child using the same configured live workspace is `shared_or_ambiguous` and carries no source revision or isolated-branch claim. Other current fork paths are `unproven`. A source workspace revision may appear only with future `derived` evidence that demonstrates actual child-workspace derivation; copying a transcript or checkpoint is not such evidence.

For Git observation on filesystems with POSIX mode support, repository configuration cannot suppress executable-bit changes. Index entries marked `assume-unchanged` or `skip-worktree` produce typed incomplete evidence instead of authorizing a false `no_change`.

For a private-argument invocation or dynamic multi-call round, the fixed
quarantine projection contains no direct-operation hashes, metadata, or
data-dependent counts and omits gap evidence. Direct reconciliation is
`not_observed`; without an overlapping window, attribution remains
conservatively `external_or_unknown` rather than claiming exact causality from
evidence that cannot be published. The process-local gap baseline is discarded
at that boundary so a later public window cannot republish quarantined state as
an external gap.

### Bounded local workspace branches

`Workspace.create_branch(WorkspaceBranchRequest(...))` is an optional capability whose compatibility default returns a typed `unsupported` result. The exact built-in `LocalWorkspace` and explicitly enabled `RunnerWorkspace` over an adapter advertising `RemoteWorkspaceBranchCapability` are the supported implementations. A successful request must carry one complete, supported revision observation for that same workspace. Creation takes exclusive cooperative ownership of the source, streams a bounded private baseline, recomputes the deterministic workspace manifest revision, and returns `conflicted` rather than opening a branch when the source no longer matches. Native remote wrappers, Git workspaces, invocation facades, arbitrary runner adapters, and unproven subclasses remain unsupported.

A `WorkspaceBranch` presents ordinary workspace reads, listings, creates, writes, conditional replacements, and deletes over a logical copy-on-write view: an immutable private baseline, changed-file overlay, and deletion tombstones. Source and sibling branches remain unchanged until publication. Returning a path to its baseline bytes removes it from the net change set; creating and deleting a branch-only path does the same. Normalizing away a private file also prunes its now-empty private ancestor directories, so transient mutations cannot bypass the configured path bound or shadow a later logical file. `changes()` returns unique path-ordered `created`, `modified`, and `deleted` entries. Its digest binds the branch ID, source workspace and observer identities, source baseline revision, operation, path, and privacy-safe before/after SHA-256 and byte-count identities. It contains no raw file content.

Publication requires a `WorkspaceBranchPublicationRequest` repeating the branch ID, baseline revision, and exact change-set digest. It freezes the overlay, takes exclusive source ownership, and validates every affected path and ancestor before the first source mutation. A created path must remain absent; modified and deleted paths must retain their baseline identities; parents must remain real directories. Any conflict returns bounded typed evidence and applies no source changes. Otherwise Cayu prepares the complete terminal result and retry receipt before mutation, applies the deterministic plan, verifies the resulting identities, and records `committed` before releasing source ownership. If source-lock teardown then hides that acknowledgement, an exact retry returns the recorded commit and the process-local source remains fenced. A failure after mutation begins restores applied paths in reverse from the immutable baseline. If restoration itself fails, Cayu preserves the ordered primary and rollback failures, fences process-local reuse, and retains the source-wide cooperative lock for the rest of the process rather than permitting uncertain writes.

Rollback never mutates the source. Explicit rollback or lifetime expiry makes the private view inaccessible, removes its storage, and releases its active-branch slot. Commit and rollback retries return the same process-local terminal result; a conflict is nonterminal and may be retried after the source is restored. Cancellation does not abandon delegated filesystem work: the public task retains its cancellation state while the owned operation settles, after which the cancellation is delivered. Creation, mutation, change evidence, active branches, and cleanup are bounded by `WorkspaceBranchLimits`; fixed-authority evidence plus request path and file limits are checked before the complete baseline observation is defensively copied. Baseline and overlay storage use a mode-`0700` sibling directory on the source workspace's filesystem, rather than the process-global temporary filesystem. A matching device alone is not sufficient: Cayu also compares supported per-directory case and Unicode lookup semantics for the source tree, baseline, and overlay. Unknown, mixed, or mismatched semantics fail before the private baseline is copied. Publication revalidates the private roots, every captured source directory, and every newly appeared affected source parent before the first source mutation. A source root with no private sibling location, an unwritable parent, or a different-device private directory likewise fails before baseline capture. A private-tree cleanup failure retains its active slot in one shared retained-cleanup registry before background scheduling; if scheduling itself is unavailable, a later creation or exact commit retry assists that retained cleanup instead of abandoning it. Traversal, aliases that the backing filesystem resolves to the same entry, symlinks, special files, root replacement, and limit violations fail closed with typed outcomes. Distinct POSIX names remain distinct branch paths even when a case-folded, Unicode-normalized, or backslash-normalized spelling would collide on another filesystem.

This is a cooperative local-filesystem transaction boundary, not a portable kernel transaction. Every Cayu `LocalWorkspace` API read, list, or mutation participates in the shared/exclusive source gate. Direct host-path access, Git-binding commands, runner commands, and unrelated same-user processes bypass that gate and are outside the atomicity guarantee; observable interference still conflicts or fences. The baseline is a bounded private byte copy plus overlay, not a Git branch, filesystem snapshot, reflink requirement, transcript/session fork, or restorable revision observation. Direct runner commands do not target the private view. Branches without durable authority retain the original process-local lifecycle and terminal receipts.

Durable local branches are an explicit opt-in. Construct `LocalWorkspace(..., branch_store=SessionWorkspaceBranchStore(session_store), branch_authority_resolver=durable_authority_provider)` and supply `branch_id`, `idempotency_key`, and `WorkspaceBranchAuthority` together on `WorkspaceBranchRequest`. Both durable boundaries must be explicit: the branch store must declare `durability="durable"`, and the authority provider must declare `claim_scope="durable"` and keep one binding-generation claim mutually exclusive across every process that can operate on the workspace. Cayu rejects durable capability claims, creation, and recovery if either boundary is process-local, development-only, read-only, or unverified. The built-in `WorkspaceBranchBindingAuthorityRegistry` truthfully declares `process_local`, so it can coordinate attached local branches but cannot activate durable recovery or retention by itself. `WorkspaceBranchStore` is the narrow workspace-owned record-journal contract; `SessionWorkspaceBranchStore` is the runtime adapter that binds it to guarded `SessionStore` transitions without making the workspace layer depend on runtime storage types, and its typed durability exactly mirrors the wrapped store's `RuntimeStoreDurability`. `InMemorySessionStore` and SQLite `:memory:` are development stores and cannot activate durable local branches; a file-backed writable SQLite store or writable PostgreSQL store declares durable storage. A custom `SessionStore` must advertise `supports_owned_off_thread_session_commit_guards=True` only when its guarded publication keeps the synchronous mutation owned through cancellation and runs it away from the asyncio event-loop thread; a subclass that overrides guarded publication must redeclare that capability for its exact implementation. The adapter rejects missing or invalid durability declarations and unsupported or merely inherited guarded-mutation claims before accepting branch state. The authority provider returns the live `WorkspaceBranchBindingAuthority` and owns generation claims; Cayu holds one exact generation claim from durable admission through private or source mutation and terminal settlement and treats that successful claim as authority evidence for that operation. A custom provider returns a transferable `WorkspaceBranchBindingAuthorityClaim`, whose idempotent `release()` may run from a later task or cleanup owner and must keep the claim active when release raises so Cayu can retain and retry it. The guarded operation neither re-enters the provider nor calls it from an off-thread commit guard while its claim is active; independent concurrent operations remain separate claims. The creation authority binds the owning session and run epoch, environment, workspace-binding generation and identity, creating authority, and resource policy. Cayu stores a digest-protected lifecycle record under a branch-derived session-operation key before creating private material. The record retains the source and baseline revision, exact root identity, limits and expiry, authority-namespaced private sibling and capture-attempt identities, overlay identities, deletion tombstones, publication or rollback authority, and a monotonic record revision. Supplying only part of this authority is rejected; reusing a branch or operation identity with different material raises `WorkspaceBranchOperationConflict`.

Creation captures the bounded baseline in one durable-attempt-scoped, owner-marked staging sibling while the store owns the guarded `creating` transition. The store runs this bounded filesystem guard outside the asyncio event-loop thread while retaining its transaction and cancellation ownership. The exact staging identity is recorded before its directory can appear, so process loss before owner-marker publication leaves at most one bounded pre-owner shape that retry can validate without recursively deleting it. Only a complete capture whose source root and live binding still match is atomically renamed, without replacement, to the durable private location before `open` commits. Process loss before that rename leaves the authoritative location absent; process loss after it leaves one complete authenticated tree that retry reconstructs. Terminal recovery derives and settles both the exact capture-attempt path and the final private path, so a failed capture whose first cleanup was interrupted cannot become an untracked staging orphan after restart. Authenticated cleanup durably records the exact opened-tree identity before atomically quarantining that pathname, so process loss while deleting the quarantine cannot turn a raced replacement into owned cleanup work. If pathname identity changes after cleanup opens the owned tree, Cayu restores the raced replacement instead of deleting it and fails closed. A reused, unmarked, or differently owned authoritative pathname is fenced and never recursively removed.

Acknowledged private mutations update the retained overlay and durable record through the store's guarded session-operation boundary. File-backed SQLite and PostgreSQL stores check the source run epoch before invoking the filesystem guard, so a replaced worker is fenced before private or source mutation. Publication first commits `publication_intent`, including an opaque source-staging owner bound to the publication identity, then applies or completes the exact frozen change set inside another guarded transition. Each affected write derives one exact staging name from that durable owner and path. Recovery removes such a name only when its bounded content identity matches the frozen after-state; mismatched staging fails closed as ambiguous, while interrupted post-write cleanup can be reconstructed before commit instead of leaving an untracked source file. Each publication key is durably bound to its first change-set digest even after a nonterminal conflict; callers must use a fresh key for new material, and `max_publication_attempts` bounds the retained ledger. A fresh owner uses `LocalWorkspace.recover_branch(WorkspaceBranchRecoveryRequest(...))` to compare each affected source path with its recorded before and after identities. All-before work is safely applied, all-after work is recognized as committed, and a before/after mixture is completed without replaying already-applied paths. An unrecognized path after partial application becomes durable `ambiguous` evidence; Cayu does not guess, roll back an external writer, delete the retained baseline/overlay, or report success. A conflict found before any source mutation remains nonterminal and returns an attached branch for an explicitly authorized retry. A source-inspection failure proven to occur before any authorized mutation becomes a durable, exactly replayable `failed` result; evidence that an earlier prefix was already applied remains `ambiguous` instead.

Rollback persists `rollback_intent` and then `rolled_back` or `expired` before private cleanup. Commit likewise persists `committed` before cleanup. A replacement process can therefore finish a lost rollback, return the exact terminal result after cleanup, or retry cleanup without losing the last proof. Before the owned private directory is renamed into its cleanup quarantine, Cayu durably records that directory's exact device/inode identity in an adjacent claim; restart cleanup deletes only a quarantine matching that positive evidence and restores a raced replacement instead. If that fresh-process terminal cleanup fails, its exact binding-generation claim transfers to a retained settlement owner and remains fenced until an assisted retry positively removes the owned tree. `creating`, `open`, publication intent/progress, committed, rollback intent, rolled back, conflicted, failed, expired, and ambiguous are distinct `WorkspaceBranchDurableState` values. Corrupt record digests, changed source-root identity, mismatched binding authority, stale run epochs, unsafe private material, and conflicting idempotency attempts fail closed. Ambiguous records intentionally retain their private evidence for operator inspection; they are not automatically made reusable.

### Remote runner workspace branches

`Workspace.branch_capabilities()` returns one typed, bounded declaration covering isolated views, deterministic net changes, cooperative atomic publication, recovery, retention, and lifecycle inspection. Every third-party and built-in adapter inherits explicit `unsupported` values. Cayu never upgrades that declaration from filesystem access, a workspace snapshot, a sync or copy binding, runner reconnectability, Git availability, or a provider claim. Application manifests (`cayu inspect`) and the server `/api/environments` control-plane response expose the same content-free declaration plus `workspace_branch_lifecycle`, a bounded snapshot of the actual states for branch handles attached to that workspace instance. The snapshot carries no branch IDs or paths, reports whether observation was truncated, and updates as attached handles move through active, publication, rollback, terminal, or fenced states. Durable lifecycle remains recoverable only by an authorized branch ID; this control-plane snapshot is not durable branch enumeration.

The first production remote implementation is `RunnerWorkspace(E2BRunner(...), enable_workspace_branches=True, ...)`. E2B opts in through the nominal `RemoteWorkspaceBranchCapability`; `E2BWorkspace`, Microsandbox, Docker, local runners, arbitrary `Runner` extensions, and a `RunnerWorkspace` without the explicit flag remain unsupported. Durable use additionally requires a `branch_authority_resolver` implementing `RemoteWorkspaceBranchAuthorityProvider` whose typed `claim_scope` is `durable`, plus the same complete `WorkspaceBranchAuthority`, publication, rollback, and recovery identities as durable local branches. Before every guest operation that provider atomically claims the complete current session/run and binding authority; a binding-only claim cannot upgrade remote recovery to durable because one environment generation may survive multiple run epochs. The provider must keep those complete claims authoritative across every worker process. The built-in `WorkspaceBranchBindingAuthorityRegistry` implements the operation-authority shape for local coordination but truthfully declares `process_local`, so it cannot upgrade a remote adapter to durable by itself. This selection is about the exact Cayu guest protocol on a retained E2B allocation, not a general claim that reconnectable sandboxes provide transactions.

The remote implementation stores a digest-protected bounded journal, immutable baseline, overlay, and tombstones in one mode-`0700` sibling directory on the allocation filesystem. Its internal `.stage` suffix is retained for the branch's complete lifecycle: Cayu never renames or removes this top-level creation directory because portable POSIX filesystems provide no pathname rename or removal conditional on an already-open directory inode. Creation first writes an immutable no-replace request-claim sidecar, creates and opens the directory, then writes a separate immutable no-replace claim that binds the request to that directory's exact device/inode before copying private bytes. Claim publication retains a hard-linked pending anchor instead of deleting a pathname after validation; a complete interrupted publication is recoverable, while an incomplete pending claim remains one capacity-bearing object for operator cleanup. Every later operation opens and locks that same inode and resolves records, blobs, temporary files, and cleanup relative to the pinned descriptor, so replacing the canonical pathname after it is pinned cannot redirect work or cause the replacement to be removed. An exact recordless or `creating` retry revalidates the source and rebuilds the same bound inode; expiry removes baseline and overlay content and writes the terminal `expired` record in that inode. The claim sidecars remain as small immutable evidence. A correlated terminal canonical record releases the capacity slot, while missing, replaced, malformed, or unbound canonical material remains capacity-bearing and untouched. POSIX has no portable atomic mkdir-and-return-directory-descriptor primitive, so interference or process loss between directory creation and its first durable inode binding cannot be distinguished safely: Cayu never adopts or removes a directory retained in that window, even when it is empty. This is a bounded fail-closed liveness leak within the direct-host-access boundary described below, not an ownership claim over hostile co-resident same-UID filesystem mutation. Overlay writes and deletes likewise record bounded before/after intent before touching private bytes; recovery settles a matching destination or owned temporary file, rolls back a provably untouched intent, and fences unindexed or contradictory private material. Limits are checked against the projected record before either mutation. Ordinary `RunnerWorkspace` operations take the shared side of a guest source lock; capture and publication take the exclusive side. Each guest operation has the bounded `branch_operation_timeout_s` configured on `RunnerWorkspace` (300 seconds by default). Publication records intent before mutation, preflights every affected path and ancestor, applies deterministic per-path atomic replacements, records progress, verifies the after identities, and only then records `committed`. A timeout, cancellation, or worker loss after durable intent never authorizes blind replay. A new Cayu process reconnecting to the same allocation compares every source path with its recorded before and after identities: it completes a provable before/after mixture, returns an existing terminal receipt, or records `ambiguous` without guessing. The record keeps its original creation authority immutable and separately advances a complete operation authority only to a strictly newer run epoch; that handoff is persisted before recovery mutates private or source state, so retry by the replacement converges while equal-epoch conflicts and older owners remain fenced. Complete invocation-authority claims fence stale run epochs and binding generations before guest work. Raw contents remain in the allocation and provider stderr, environment data, credentials, allocation IDs, and unrestricted command output are never copied into public branch evidence.

The atomicity boundary is cooperative across Cayu workspace operations on that exact root. A co-resident process or direct runner command can bypass the source lock; detected interference conflicts before publication or makes interrupted recovery ambiguous. The guarantee is not a filesystem-wide transaction, VM snapshot, portable process image, cross-provider migration, Git operation, or proof about provider infrastructure beyond the retained allocation. A process-local creator whose success acknowledgement is lost has no reconstructable handle; its positively bound private record remains capacity-bearing only until the configured branch lifetime, and the next creation settles that expiry before capacity admission. The pre-bind fail-closed case above is the exception: its directory and claim remain capacity-bearing until an operator investigates and removes both. Deterministic CI runs the same shared branch suite through an explicit fake remote capability, while `tests/workspaces/test_e2b_workspace_branches_e2e.py` is the opt-in live proof (`CAYU_RUN_E2B_WORKSPACE_BRANCH_E2E=1`).

Each window captures a bounded before observation in memory, then—only after the invocation secret scope is sealed—durably emits `workspace.revision.observed` for before and after execution followed by `workspace.mutation.recorded`. This prevents a secret resolved during execution from appearing retroactively in already-published path, branch, revision, or artifact evidence. A private-argument invocation or dynamic multi-call round publishes fixed content-free truncated evidence rather than allowing receipt fields to bypass its publication quarantine. The records link the session run epoch, model step and attempt, tool round and call, workspace identity, window identity, and before/after event ids. Observations declare whether their path evidence is a complete inventory or a changed-path view, so a Git-dirty path becoming clean is not misreported as a filesystem deletion. Git observation combines a bounded complete index inventory with changed and untracked worktree entries. Ignored paths are excluded before path counting and content reads, so dependency caches and credential-like files outside Git's observable source set cannot suppress or fingerprint the receipt. This retains path attribution when a tool commits a clean-baseline tracked change while avoiding reads of every clean tracked file. Git rename detection is requested explicitly, submodule ignore configuration is overridden, and an unambiguous committed rename is reconstructed from the stable index object identity when status output cannot describe the historical source path. Mutable symlink or submodule worktree states fail as incomplete when the adapter cannot collect non-following evidence safely. Repository-configured fsmonitor and hooks, ambient Git repository and tracing overrides, optional locks, and global/system configuration are disabled during observation. Deltas distinguish `changed`, `no_change`, `unsupported`, `failed`, `incomplete`, and `truncated`; malformed, duplicate-path, or identity-drifting observer output becomes a typed capture failure without replacing the tool's own outcome. Runtime hard caps are re-applied to custom observer output before it is detached or projected; built-in collection defaults to at most 8 MiB per file and 64 MiB across one observation, and an over-limit result becomes typed truncation. Each custom observer call is owned independently and bounded to 30 seconds; timeout or observer-owned cancellation becomes fixed capture-failure evidence, while authenticated caller cancellation propagates. A still-running observer remains retained in a bounded registry and on the environment fence until it settles, so binding finalization or later environment reuse cannot race its workspace access. An observer-owned cancellation is not positive quiescence evidence even when its coroutine has terminated: because the public observer contract cannot prove that opaque delegated work stopped, the environment remains quarantined rather than authorizing later mutation or finalization. Inline evidence is content-free, redacted, and bounded by path and serialized-byte limits. Larger manifests use a session-scoped artifact reference with an expected SHA-256 and byte size. A local artifact store rooted inside the observed local workspace is ineligible for receipt-manifest externalization, because the evidence write would contaminate the exclusive tool window; the observation is visibly truncated instead, while the tool continues to receive its configured store. Missing or ineligible artifact storage, output truncation, unsafe paths, symlink escapes, unreadable files, and byte/path/manifest limit breaches fail closed with typed status and fixed detail codes rather than publishing file contents or external exception text. Once the tool has returned, capture or receipt-publication failure cannot erase its authoritative terminal outcome: the terminal event carries a fixed `workspace_mutation_capture_status` and optional detail code, and post-tool receipt events are not exposed to the stream consumer until terminal evidence has been durably recorded or staged.

Receipt-manifest artifact writes use the same 30-second owned-operation ceiling. A timed-out or caller-abandoned write remains retained and observed within the bounded capture registry and the environment's mutation fence until it settles, but it cannot delay the tool's terminal result; a late process-control outcome remains attached to that retained owner instead of being discarded. The receipt records fixed truncation evidence and preserves the artifact intent rather than claiming that a cancellation-opaque write failed. Once artifact-store dispatch begins, any returned failure is likewise acknowledgement-ambiguous and leaves the durable intent open; only authoritative no-dispatch evidence may mark that write failed. The stable artifact ID, digest, size, store identity, and `intent` state make a late or commit-then-raise successful write an explicit possible orphan instead of an untracked object.

Each workspace mutation window also owns a versioned `workspace_observations` checkpoint record. Its first transition stamps the current root checkpoint schema in the same atomic publication, and ordinary `SessionStore.checkpoint(...)` or generic transform callbacks cannot replace or delete the runtime-owned observation root; only the scoped recovery path may advance it outside a typed publication. Its immutable authority tuple binds the session and source run epoch, binding generation, workspace and observer identities, artifact-store identity, model step and attempt, tool round and call, and stable window ID. Before the initial intent is persisted, configured workspace, artifact-store, and extension-observer identities cross a private secret-admission boundary. Dynamic environments retain configurable identities only as field- and session-scoped keyed aliases because their complete invocation secret set is not yet available; exact built-in observer identities carry an explicit `runtime_builtin` provenance discriminator rather than being reclassified from string equality. Fresh-process recovery requires that discriminator to match the current binding's exact built-in type, while configured extensions cannot inherit it by using the same class name. An unmaterialized factory registration is not evidence about its previous concrete workspace or binding: recovery authenticates the retained session/profile/tool-round tuple, does not call the factory or any observation extension merely to reconstruct evidence, and closes the lifecycle with bounded incomplete or ambiguous evidence when the historical authority is unavailable. Persistent stores therefore require the same public-authority alias keyring used by all workers before a dynamic workspace-mutation intent can be admitted. Compare-and-set `workspace-observation` publications advance that record through intent, before capture, durably staged tool outcome, after capture, delta/artifact publication, and terminal removal. Every phase has a stable publication ID and the store checks the current run epoch and prior root digest atomically, so acknowledgement replay converges and a stale worker cannot publish for a replacement run or binding. A malformed or lost acknowledgement is reconciled only through the immutable exact receipt and retained request; caller cancellation is preserved across committed-result validation and persisted-event fan-out, so it cannot turn a committed transition into missing public evidence. If both the initial publication and reconciliation fail, their ordered original exceptions remain attached exactly once to the authoritative cancellation or failure. The authoritative tool terminal event is content-bound independently of its mutable capture-status fields: revision failure never erases or changes the tool outcome, and observation recovery never reruns the tool, runner command, provider request, hook, or other external effect.

Fresh-process incomplete-session recovery closes every surviving observation record before ordinary tool-round repair. Intent or before-only records become `workspace.observation.finalized` with `ambiguous`; a durable tool outcome without complete after/delta evidence becomes `incomplete`; a complete durable delta is verified and finalized without observing the current workspace or assigning later changes to the original tool. A terminal recovery event without a verified mutation receipt carries explicit `external_or_unknown` (or `concurrent_ambiguity` for an ambiguous lifecycle) attribution with unknown isolation and no direct-operation claim. When an unmaterialized factory leaves the historical concrete observation authority unavailable, even complete retained delta evidence is finalized as incomplete rather than being upgraded through a replacement environment. The recovery action is `repaired_workspace_observation`. Competing workers use the session recovery claim plus run-epoch/CAS transitions and therefore converge on one terminal event. Missing or conflicting content-bound tool evidence fails closed as ambiguous rather than authorizing reconstructed causality.

Artifact publication is tracked as intent, published, referenced, failed, orphaned, or missing. Recovery reads an artifact only from the exact stable artifact-store identity recorded before dispatch, enforces its recorded byte size, and verifies its ID, filename, media type, scope, session/agent/environment ownership, evidence kind, window ID, SHA-256, and metadata before retaining a reference. A published artifact with no committed event reference is reported as orphaned and is preserved for explicit backend/operator cleanup; recovery does not delete it by pathname or guess ownership. An absent intent remains `intent`, because a cancellation-opaque write can become visible after recovery's read; the final event retains its exact artifact ID, digest, size, and store identity for explicit cleanup. A referenced artifact that is absent or fails integrity verification makes the terminal observation incomplete. This is deliberate bounded consistency across the session store and `ArtifactStore`, not a distributed transaction.

Terminal environment binding finalization performs one separately bounded revision observation after mutation-quiescence fencing and before the binding's final mutation or synchronization step. If a custom final observer does not settle after its deadline or caller abandonment, its exact task transfers to the environment mutation fence; binding finalization, abandonment, and later reuse remain blocked until that task positively settles. For an environment with a positively static secret-resolution scope, `environment.binding.finalize.completed.final_revision` reports the last safely observable workspace ID, observer, status, revision, HEAD, branch, scope, count, and fixed detail code. Its nested `finalization_delta` compares that state with the latest durable after-window observation. Changes after the last window are bounded, path-hashed, and classified `unattributed_finalization_change`; no tool-call or mutation-window identity is attached. Missing or externalized baseline paths produce explicit incomplete/truncated delta evidence rather than a fabricated path list. A vault-, proxy-, or factory-backed environment instead publishes fixed content-free `truncated` revision and finalization-delta evidence with no revision, HEAD, branch, or path identity and omits the sibling final snapshot: terminal finalization may run after the invocation redactor has been discarded or in a fresh process, so it cannot reconstruct dynamic secrets safely in either representation. If the subsequent binding finalization or finalize-completion publication fails, the same bounded safe projection is retained on the failure evidence and terminal session event instead of being discarded.

The user-input prompt visibility described above requires a statically complete durable secret scope. When the environment can resolve secrets dynamically, or a legacy checkpoint has no positive scope evidence, the private checkpoint retains the original `question`, `options`, and per-call policy output for continuation, but public pause events omit the prompt and per-call `reason`/`metadata`. Pending-action projections use `question=null`, `options=[]`, and the fixed detail `Input required`. If continuation reconstructs a policy-denied sibling, its blocked output likewise uses fixed diagnostics unless the durable scope is positively static. This fail-closed projection prevents a sibling tool from later establishing that an already-published prompt or policy output was a workload secret.

A pending round that was durably classified as static cannot be continued after the same registered environment changes to dynamic secret resolution. Cayu rejects that capability upgrade before claiming or mutating the interrupted session because the earlier public prompt or policy fields cannot be recalled. Manual approval, user-input, and ordinary tool-round recovery also require positive static-scope evidence before publishing operator-supplied result, reason, or metadata fields. Dynamic or legacy/unknown recovery retains the operator's completed/failed classification but publishes a fixed unavailable result and empty audit text instead.

Policy output follows the same positive-evidence rule because a custom policy receives private tool arguments and may derive its `reason` or `metadata` from them. A statically complete round retains the existing bounded public policy output. An ordinary denial in a dynamic or legacy/unknown round uses fixed denial diagnostics in its blocked event, hook result, transcript result, and export, so a sibling cannot resolve the same value after argument-derived policy output has already been published. A dynamic or legacy/unknown approval round keeps policy output only in the private approval checkpoint: `tool.call.approval_requested`, the nested `session.interrupted` approval, recovery events, and per-call descriptors omit `reason` and `metadata`, while pending actions use the fixed detail `Approval required`. If approval closure reconstructs a denied sibling, it uses the same fixed denial diagnostics. Approval identity, policy evidence, expiry, and private continuation state remain available.

Manual tool-round recovery installs an `incomplete_session_recovery_claim` in
the same transaction that transitions the session to `RUNNING` and advances its
run epoch. The claim is heartbeated through continuation, blocks recovery on
other workers, and permits an expired owner to be fenced without replaying its
operator-supplied outcome. Heartbeat loss cancels the continuation and completes
session and environment cleanup before releasing durable ownership. If either
the initial claim transition or an atomic expired-owner takeover has an
ambiguous acknowledgement, Cayu reconciles both its preassigned claim identity
and the run epoch created by that claim; a replacement owner's checkpoint is
not adopted or cleaned up as if it belonged to the failed caller. Caller
cancellation remains authoritative, and a reconciled takeover claim is released
before the original transport/store error returns, so it cannot block an
immediate retry. If a claimed recovery of an orphaned `RUNNING` or
`INTERRUPTING` session finds durable
evidence or otherwise fails before writing a new outcome, Cayu closes the
session to `INTERRUPTED` rather than restoring a stale live status; ordinary
`resume(...)` can then finish from the event ledger. The process-local recovery
supervisor remains cancellable while the consumer is paused between events. It
also polls durable interruption status at a bounded interval for the lifetime
of this rare manual-recovery operation, using the terminal interruption present
before the claim as its baseline. The watcher reacts to `INTERRUPTING` or a
newer explicit `operator_requested` terminal event, but not to the recovery's
own resumable `runtime_interrupted` transition. This allows
`interrupt_session(...)` on a different API worker to stop the owner without
waiting for another stream read.
A concurrent interruption therefore stops the owned continuation and finalizes
the existing durable operator request, including its reason, metadata, and
request identity. If that request reaches `INTERRUPTING` before the atomic
recovery claim—or reaches `INTERRUPTED` after the recovery request loaded its
session snapshot—interruption wins: recovery does not transition the session
back to `RUNNING`, and the verified tool outcome remains unapplied for a later
explicit retry. The same rule applies when the pending operator-interruption
marker already exists at the initial snapshot: recovery repairs a missing
terminal interruption event before returning. Manual recovery also refuses its
atomic claim while `pending_interruption_cascade` exists, so it cannot complete
a parent session while descendant interruption is still being reconciled. The
interruption fence installs a preassigned durable claim so commit-acknowledgement
failures can be reconciled and cleaned up exactly.

Policy requests receive copied session, agent, tool-call, argument, declared `tool_effect`, environment, workspace, and metadata values. Mutating a policy request does not mutate the tool arguments that may later reach the tool. Runtime tools receive copied request metadata through `ToolContext.metadata`, plus runtime-owned call identity keys such as `tool_call_id`, `idempotency_key`, `tool_effect`, `approval_id`, and `input_id`; runtime-owned keys win on collision.

## Event

Append-only event emitted by the runtime for sessions, model steps, tools, workflows, memory, runners, and storage-visible lifecycle changes.
Runtime event types are enumerated. Extension events must use the `custom.` namespace so typos do not silently become durable event names.

Events power:

- terminal output
- dashboard
- webhooks
- session replay
- hosted platform adapters
- tests and debugging

Every run/resume invocation emits `turn.completed` before the terminal session event when the runtime reaches a normal completed, failed, interrupted, or limit-interrupted outcome. The payload is derived from durable usage-bearing events in that invocation: `status`, `duration_ms`, `step_count`, `tool_call_count`, `token_usage`, `provider_names`, `models`, and `interaction_ids`. `turn.completed.interaction_id` is null because one invocation can consume queued input and produce more than one response. Consumers that need response-scoped evidence use the interaction contract below; detailed usage/cost APIs still derive from durable model/tool events and remain the source for historical reports.

### Conversation interactions

Interaction lifecycle summaries carry provider and model name lists as insertion-ordered sets:
distinct values retain their first-observed order, and duplicate entries are invalid durable
evidence.

A session contains many durable interactions. One interaction starts with the user-input batch that is eligible to produce one assistant response and contains every model step, retry, tool round, transcript record, pause, continuation, and runtime event that contributes to that response. `interaction_id` is distinct from session, mutation, run-epoch, tool-round, operation, and provider response identity.

Initial run messages and ordinary resume messages start new interactions. Tool approval and required user input pause the current interaction and later resolutions retain its identity. Queued input that is already eligible before the first provider step joins the not-yet-dispatched interaction. Once an interaction has produced model or tool work, a delivered `next_turn` or `on_idle` batch waits for that interaction's terminal assistant response and starts a new interaction, even when delivery and the next response happen inside the same public runtime invocation. Parallel tool calls keep their own `tool_call_id` and `tool_round_id` while sharing the interaction ID. Explicit idle operations such as application-requested compaction remain intentionally unassociated.

Runtime events and provider-neutral transcript records expose nullable first-class `interaction_id` fields. Built-in stores persist and index those fields; null is reserved for intentionally unassociated runtime evidence and is never inferred from timestamps or adjacency. The explicit runtime-event allow-list is the invocation-scoped `turn.completed` event and the session-scoped events `session.completed`, `session.failed`, `session.interrupted`, and `runtime.interaction_transition.acknowledgement_failed`; the acknowledgement diagnostic spans transition attempts and cancellation settlement, while its committed interaction outcome is already represented by the immutable transition receipt and lifecycle event.
